clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive disorder of pulmonary surfactant metabolism caused by biallelic SFTPB mutations
Typically presents in term newborns with severe, progressive respiratory distress unresponsive to conventional surfactant replacement
It is a leading inherited cause of fatal neonatal respiratory failure of unclear initial cause
Chest imaging resembles neonatal respiratory distress syndrome despite the infant being at term
Diagnosis rests on genetic testing, with supportive lung histology and absent mature surfactant protein B
Lung transplantation is the only definitive treatment, as the deficiency is not corrected by exogenous surfactant
Carrier parents are usually asymptomatic, and recurrence risk in future pregnancies is significant
reference.pathophysiology: Surfactant protein B is essential for the formation and stability of the surfactant film that lowers alveolar surface tension. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in SFTPB abolish functional protein, so surfactant cannot organise normally and lamellar bodies are malformed. The result is widespread alveolar collapse, impaired gas exchange and a histological pattern of alveolar proteinosis with accumulated abnormal surfactant material. Because the defect is intrinsic to surfactant assembly, exogenous surfactant provides only transient benefit, and progressive respiratory failure ensues.
additionalDifferentials: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome of prematurity
Congenital alveolar proteinosis of other cause
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
additionalInvestigations: Chest imaging showing a diffuse ground-glass or granular pattern
Lung biopsy with immunostaining for surfactant proteins when needed
Assessment for the common recurrent SFTPB mutation
Exclusion of infection and structural cardiac disease
redFlags: Severe respiratory failure in a term neonate without another cause
Poor or only transient response to exogenous surfactant
Rapidly progressive hypoxaemia requiring escalating support
Family history of unexplained neonatal respiratory death
reference.prognosis: Classic complete surfactant protein B deficiency is usually fatal in infancy without lung transplantation; partial or milder variants may have a more protracted course.
pitfalls: Attributing term-infant respiratory failure solely to infection or transient tachypnoea
Assuming failure to respond to surfactant excludes a surfactant disorder
Delaying genetic testing in unexplained severe neonatal lung disease
Overlooking the recurrence risk and the value of genetic counselling
references: Kendig's Disorders of the Respiratory Tract in Children (standard reference)
management: Definitive treatment is lung transplantation, since exogenous surfactant replacement gives only transient benefit and cannot correct the intrinsic surfactant protein B defect
Provide intensive respiratory support with mechanical ventilation and oxygen, using exogenous surfactant only as a temporising measure
Consider extracorporeal membrane oxygenation as a bridge to transplantation in refractory respiratory failure
Optimise nutrition and growth and treat intercurrent infection promptly to keep the infant transplant-eligible
Monitor gas exchange and screen for pulmonary hypertension with serial echocardiography
Coordinate care across neonatology, paediatric respiratory medicine and a lung transplant centre
Offer genetic counselling with carrier and family testing given autosomal recessive inheritance, and discuss prenatal testing in future pregnancies
Introduce palliative care and honest prognostic discussion where transplantation is not feasible
